title: William Penn's Treaty Under the Elm
text:
In 1681 King Charles II granted William Penn, a Quaker, a vast territory in America to repay a debt owed to Penn's father. Penn named it Pennsylvania and planned it as a "holy experiment" in religious freedom. Unlike many colonizers, he held that the land belonged to the Lenape people who lived there, and that it should be bought from them, not simply taken.

According to tradition, in late 1682 Penn met Lenape leaders, among them the chief Tamanend, under a great elm tree at Shackamaxon, on the Delaware River near what became Philadelphia. There, the story goes, they made a treaty of friendship, promising to live in peace for as long as the rivers flowed and the sun shone.

No written text of such a treaty survives, and historians think the tradition may combine several agreements. But Penn did deal with the Lenape fairly by the standards of his time, and Pennsylvania had no war with them for decades. Voltaire praised it as the only treaty never sworn to and never broken, and Benjamin West's famous painting made the scene an American icon.

After Penn's death his sons cheated the Lenape in the Walking Purchase of 1737, and the peace broke down.
lesson: Fair dealing with neighbors can keep the peace for generations. Trust built over years can be destroyed in one dishonest bargain.
source: Pennsylvania tradition; Voltaire, Letters on the English (1733), letter 4
caveat: No document of the treaty survives, and its details are traditional.
